passage: "Your 'quick' lunch," said Himani, drawing quote marks in the air, "lasted forty minutes." Pallavi burst out laughing and threw a napkin at her. Later, when Pallavi was named class captain, Himani snapped a mock salute across the corridor. "Yes, captain!" Pallavi bowed dramatically. Then a girl from another section passed them and said, "Oh, you two are 'friends'," with the same finger quotes and a flat look. Pallavi's smile dropped. Himani noticed and stepped closer. "That one wasn't a joke," she said. "Ignore her. Want to walk together?" The same gesture, three completely different meanings.

qa.q: How long did Himani say Pallavi's lunch lasted?
qa.a: She said it lasted forty minutes.

qa.q: What was Pallavi feeling when the girl from the other section said 'friends'?
qa.a: Pallavi felt hurt because the finger quotes and flat look sounded like a put-down. Pallavi's smile dropped, unlike when Himani was the one teasing.

qa.q: What could Himani do if she uses air quotes with someone she doesn't know well?
qa.a: She could check the person's face and add a smile or a few clear words. Tone decides whether it reads as teasing.

qa.q: How does the girl from another section's gesture differ for Pallavi from Himani's?
qa.a: Himani's air quotes and salute came with laughter and warmth, so they felt like friendly teasing. The other girl's came with a flat look, so they felt like a dig.

grounding: A teenager's air quotes and mock salute are friendly teasing or a put-down depending on tone.

"Your 'study group' looked a lot like a party," Ankita said, curling her fingers in the air.
"Excuse me?" said Jyoti.
"Kidding! Well, mostly. Loud music, pizza boxes."
"Was that a joke or a dig?"
"A joke. Why?"
"It didn't sound like one. You didn't smile."
Ankita paused. "Oh. I was tired. Sorry, it landed wrong."
"We actually did study. For an hour."
"Good. Then salute to the hour." She gave a small, silly salute.
Jyoti laughed. "Okay, that one I liked. Now you can drop the quote marks." 🙂

qa.q: What did Ankita say the study group looked like?
qa.a: She said it looked a lot like a party.

qa.q: What was Jyoti feeling when she asked whether it was a joke or a dig?
qa.a: Jyoti was unsure and a bit hurt because Ankita did not smile. The direct question shows Jyoti wanted to check before assuming.

qa.q: What worked in this conversation?
qa.a: Jyoti asked outright whether it was a joke, and Ankita explained and apologised. Naming the tone cleared the confusion.

qa.q: How might Ankita see the same air quotes?
qa.a: Ankita meant it as a joke, but she was tired and forgot to smile. She sees now that her tone made it land wrong.

grounding: A teenager's air quotes and mock salute may be teasing or a put-down, and tone decides.

passage:
In Class 9, when Sonali presented her science project, I made air quotes and said, "Her 'amazing' project." Everyone laughed.
I thought it was funny. But Sonali's face dropped. She finished her presentation, but her voice was shaky.
Later, she came up to me. "Why did you do that? I worked on it for two weeks."
I felt terrible. I said sorry. I told her I didn't think about how it would feel.
Now when I use air quotes, I think first. They can make a joke, but they can also make someone feel small.
- Kunal

qa.q: How long did Sonali work on her project?
qa.a: Two weeks.

qa.q: What was Sonali feeling when Kunal made air quotes?
qa.a: Sonali felt hurt and embarrassed, since the air quotes mocked her hard work.

qa.q: What did Kunal learn to do differently?
qa.a: Kunal learned to think before using air quotes, because they can put someone down.

qa.q: How might the classmates who laughed see the air quotes now?
qa.a: They might realise the air quotes were a put-down, not just a joke.

grounding: The narrator recalls using air quotes to mock a classmate's project and learning that tone decides if they are teasing or hurtful.

passage:
Teacher's note, Monday
When I assigned the weekend essay, Shankar stood up and gave me a big mock salute. "Yes, ma'am!" Everyone laughed, including me. His grin was friendly, and he started the essay right away.
Later, though, when Priyanka shared her idea for the class trip, Shankar made air quotes: "'Great' idea." Priyanka went quiet.
I spoke to him after class. I told him the salute was funny because it was friendly, but the air quotes felt like a put-down.
He looked surprised. "I was joking."
"It didn't feel like a joke to Priyanka," I said.
Tomorrow he's going to talk to her.
- Ms Devika

qa.q: What did Shankar say when he saluted?
qa.a: "Yes, ma'am!"

qa.q: What was Priyanka feeling when Shankar made air quotes?
qa.a: Priyanka felt hurt and embarrassed, reading the air quotes as mockery of her idea.

qa.q: What did Ms Devika do that helped?
qa.a: She pointed out the difference in tone between the friendly salute and the mocking air quotes, and encouraged Shankar to talk to Priyanka.

qa.q: How might Shankar see his own gestures after the talk?
qa.a: Shankar might realise that even jokes can hurt, depending on tone and who they're aimed at.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a teenager using a friendly mock salute and hurtful air quotes, showing tone decides the meaning.

passage:
Friday
I won the inter-school debate today!! My hands were still shaking from the last rebuttal when I came off stage. Jahnavi was waiting at the steps and gave me a big, slow, serious salute, then burst out grinning. It felt like she was really proud of me, like I was a general coming back from battle.
But then in the canteen, someone from the other team said, "Here comes the 'winner,'" doing air quotes. My stomach dropped.
Jahnavi saw my face. She said loudly, "Yes, the real winner," and saluted again.
I laughed, and the knot in my stomach went away. Same kind of gesture, both done with fingers in the air, but one was a put-down and one was respect. It all depends on the face and the voice that come with it.
- Jaya

qa.q: What did Jahnavi do when Jaya came off stage?
qa.a: She gave a big salute, grinning.

qa.q: What was Jaya feeling when the other team used air quotes?
qa.a: Jaya felt hurt and deflated, since the air quotes made the win seem fake.

qa.q: What did Jahnavi do that helped?
qa.a: Jahnavi countered the put-down by saying "the real winner" and saluting again, showing respect.

qa.q: How might the student from the other team have seen the air quotes?
qa.a: They may have been disappointed about losing and used the air quotes to feel better, not caring how it hurt.

grounding: A teenager's diary shows a friendly salute as respect and air quotes as a put-down, with tone deciding meaning.
